title: Nala and Damayanti
hook: Yudhishthira asks if any king was ever more unlucky, and a sage begins the story of Nala and a golden swan

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Arjuna's austerities: a door in Indra's city, a refusal, and a curse that would one day hide him. When did a pause change something for you? Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

Back in the forest, Arjuna is gone, and his brothers miss him. Yudhishthira is the one who threw the dice, and he can't stop going over it. So when a sage named Brihadashva visits the camp, Yudhishthira asks him a question that sounds like a complaint and is really a plea. Has there ever been a king more unlucky than me? The sage doesn't argue with him. He doesn't give him a lecture. He tells him a story. There was a king, he says, who also lost his kingdom at dice. His name was Nala. And the story begins, of all places, with a bird.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA'S QUESTION.` → `"MORE UNLUCKY THAN ME?"` → `THE SAGE TELLS A STORY.`

segments.voice: Nala is the king of the Nishadhas: handsome, learned, truthful, and a master with horses. Far away, in Vidarbha, lives Damayanti, the daughter of King Bhima, and the story praises her beauty in line after line. The two have never met. But people talk, and each keeps hearing about the other, and each begins to love someone they have never seen. One day, in a garden, Nala catches a swan with wings that shine like gold. The swan speaks. Let me go, it says, and I'll praise you to Damayanti so well she'll think of no one else. Nala lets it go. The swan flies to Vidarbha and lands among Damayanti and her friends, and when she reaches for it, it speaks to her of Nala. Damayanti's answer is simple: say the same of me to him. So a bird carries love back and forth between two people who live in different kingdoms. Then Damayanti grows pale and quiet, and her father notices. He decides it's time for her swayamvara, the ceremony where a princess chooses her own husband, and kings start arriving from every direction. Now step back and see why the sage tells this story here. Yudhishthira wants to know if his suffering is the worst there has ever been. The sage answers with a love story that starts in a garden. He's asking Yudhishthira to listen all the way to the end. A story can hold a grief long enough for someone to see it from a little distance. So we'll stay with Nala and Damayanti for a while, the way Yudhishthira did.
screen: `NALA, KING OF THE NISHADHAS.` · `DAMAYANTI OF VIDARBHA.` · `A GOLDEN SWAN CARRIES THE NEWS.` · then, large: `A STORY TO HOLD A GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and let the breath slow down without forcing it. Bring to mind a story someone once told you when you were struggling: a parent, a friend, a teacher, a book. You may not remember all of it. Remember how it felt to be handed it. Breathe in, and hold that memory gently. Breathe out, and let a little thanks go toward whoever told it. If you pray, you can remember that person in your prayer. If not, simply stay with the memory of being told a story. The bell holds the time.
Nala and Damayanti. Two people who love each other before they meet, carried to each other by a golden swan, told to a grieving king in the forest.
Your line: Nala and Damayanti. Today, when someone tells you a hard thing, see whether a story would help more than advice. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: The story of Nala and Damayanti is told within the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, by the sage Brihadashva to Yudhishthira, and it is also retold on its own.

fork.setup: you're Nala. you've caught a golden swan, and it begs to be set free, promising to praise you to Damayanti. what do you do?
options: keep it, it's too beautiful to lose.
send it to your own court as a gift.
fork.reveal: he lets it go, and the swan flies to Vidarbha and speaks of Nala to Damayanti.

original.note: Sanskrit Damayanti, the princess of Vidarbha whose story the sage tells to Yudhishthira.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nala and Damayanti is a love story dropped into the epic.
what it means: a sage tells it to Yudhishthira, a king who also lost everything at dice.
what a scholar hears: the epic places stories inside stories, and the frame tells you why this one is being told.
